    Geospatial Python Basics

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How does Python store and map geographic data?
    • What is a coordinate reference system, and why does it matter for measuring?
    • How do I combine a table with a map layer, or two layers with each other?
    • How is raster data different from vector data, and how do I read it?

    Objectives

    • Read vector data from the web into a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame and map it
    • Check, convert and correctly label a layer’s coordinate reference system
    • Measure areas and distances in meters
    • Combine data with attribute joins and spatial joins
    • Read a raster with rasterio, summarize its cells and clip it to a polygon

    Vector data and GeoDataFrames

    Most social science maps use vector data: points (a store, a survey respondent), lines (a road, a river) and polygons (a county, a census tract). Each feature has a shape and a row of attributes.

    GeoPandas stores vector data as a GeoDataFrame: a pandas DataFrame with one extra geometry column. Everything from the previous episode (selecting, filtering, sorting, new columns) still works, and maps are one line away.

    PYTHON 

    import geopandas as gpd

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/Foundations/main/data/indiana_counties.geojson"
counties = gpd.read_file(url)
counties.plot(column="unemp_2016", cmap="YlOrRd", legend=True)

    gpd.read_file() reads GeoJSON, shapefiles (also zipped ones) and GeoPackages, from a file or a web address. Shade areas by rates (unemployment, density), not raw counts, or big counties will dominate the map simply because they are big.

    Coordinate reference systems

    Coordinates are only numbers; the coordinate reference system (CRS) says what they mean. Web data is usually in EPSG:4326: latitude and longitude, in degrees. Degrees are fine for storing data, but a degree of longitude shrinks from about 111 km at the equator to about 85 km in Indiana, so areas and distances calculated in degrees are meaningless.

    Method What it does When to use it
    layer.crs Shows the CRS Always, before combining or measuring layers
    layer.to_crs(epsg=26916) Converts the coordinates to another CRS Before measuring, or to match another layer
    layer.set_crs(epsg=4326) Labels a layer whose CRS is missing; the numbers do not change Only when the CRS is missing and you know what it should be

    For Indiana, EPSG:26916 (UTM zone 16N, in meters) is a good choice for local distances, and EPSG:5070 (USA Contiguous Albers Equal Area) for areas across the state or the country. The Data Management module’s Coordinate Reference Systems episode explains datums and projections in depth.

    Joining data

    Join Matches rows by GeoPandas
    Attribute join A shared ID, such as a FIPS code or GEOID layer.merge(table, on="fips")
    Spatial join Location: which polygon contains each point gpd.sjoin(points, polygons, predicate="within")

    The most common reason an attribute join fails is that the ID is text in one table and a number in the other. Convert both to text (and pad with zfill() to the right length) before joining, and always compare the row counts before and after. A spatial join needs both layers in the same CRS.

    Raster data

    A raster covers an area with a grid of equal cells, each holding one number: an elevation, a temperature, a satellite reflectance, or a class code such as “forest”. Rasters suit things that vary continuously across space, while vector data suits discrete features.

    Vector Raster
    Stores Features with shapes and attributes A grid of cells, one value per cell per band
    Detail set by The accuracy of the shapes The cell size (resolution), for example 30 m
    Typical files GeoJSON, shapefile, GeoPackage GeoTIFF
    Python library GeoPandas rasterio (with NumPy)

    Every raster also has a CRS, an extent and a no-data value that marks cells with no measurement. Read the cells with masked=True so that value does not distort your statistics.

    PYTHON 

    import rasterio

dem = rasterio.open("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/Foundations/main/data/tippecanoe_dem.tif")
print(dem.crs, dem.res, dem.nodata)
elev = dem.read(1, masked=True)      # a NumPy array of elevations in meters
print(elev.min(), elev.max())

    Some rasters hold measurements (elevation, temperature): averages and histograms make sense. Others are categorical (land cover codes): count the cells of each class instead, because the average of “forest” and “water” means nothing. The Data Management module’s Geospatial Data Models episode compares the two data models in more depth.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: set_crs or to_crs?

    1. A shapefile arrives with no CRS. Its metadata says the coordinates are latitude and longitude (WGS 84).
    2. You need the distance in meters between two stores stored in EPSG:4326.
    3. One layer is in EPSG:4326 and another in EPSG:26916, and you want to draw them together.
    1. set_crs(epsg=4326): the CRS is missing and you know what it is, so you only add the label.
    2. to_crs(epsg=26916) first, then measure: the coordinates must be converted to meters.
    3. to_crs() one layer to match the other, for example layer2.to_crs(layer1.crs).
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Why did the join fail?

    You join a table of tract statistics to tract boundaries on GEOID, and every row of the result has empty statistics. What would you check first?

    Check the type and format of GEOID in both tables. A common cause is that one table stores it as text ("18157010400") and the other as a number (18157010400), or that leading zeros were lost (a California tract "06001400100" read as the number 6001400100). Convert both to text with .astype(str).str.zfill(11) (11 characters for tracts) and join again. Also check that both tables cover the same year, because tract boundaries change between censuses.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Vector or raster?

    Which data model would you choose for each, and why?

    1. The locations of 17 supermarkets
    2. Air temperature across Indiana at 2 p.m.
    3. Land cover (forest, crops, water, developed) for a county
    4. Census tract boundaries with their population
    1. Vector (points): a few discrete features with attributes such as a name.
    2. Raster: temperature varies continuously, so a grid of values fits.
    3. Usually raster (as in the NLCD land cover in notebook 4d), because satellites classify every cell. It can be converted to polygons, but the files grow large.
    4. Vector (polygons): tracts are discrete areas with attributes.
    Key Points
    • A GeoDataFrame is a pandas DataFrame plus a geometry column; gpd.read_file() reads it from the web
    • Check .crs first; use to_crs() to a projected CRS in meters before measuring, and set_crs() only to label missing CRS information
    • Attribute joins match IDs (make them the same type first); spatial joins match locations (same CRS first)
    • A raster is a grid of cells with a CRS, a cell size and a no-data value; rasterio reads it into a NumPy array

    Notebooks

    Notebook What you will do
    4a. Vector Data with GeoPandas Read Indiana counties and Lafayette food stores, make a choropleth and layer points over polygons
    4b. Coordinate Reference Systems Compare areas in degrees and meters, measure a distance, and see what a wrong CRS label does
    4c. Joining Tables and Layers Fix a failing FIPS join, then find which stores lie inside the city limits
    4d. Raster Data with rasterio Read Tippecanoe County elevation and land cover, look up values at points, and clip land cover to the cities
